articles.title: Before He Reached The Supreme Court, A Mob Nearly Got To Him First
articles.content:
Ed. Note: Welcome to our daily feature Trivia Question of the Day!

Long before Thurgood Marshall won Brown v. Board of Education or took his seat as the first Black justice of the Supreme Court, he spent years as the NAACP’s traveling trial lawyer, defending Black clients in some of the most dangerous corners of the Jim Crow South. In 1946, one of those trips nearly cost him his life: after a courtroom victory in a small Southern town, local police stopped his car, arrested him on a bogus charge, and drove him toward a river where a mob was waiting. What state was he in?

Hint: The town sits about 30 miles from the birthplace of the Ku Klux Klan. He lived only because his fellow lawyers refused to leave his side.

See the answer on the next page.

articles.title: Food, Shelter, Or Taxes: How Inflation Is Making Making Taxpayers Choose Between Survival And Their Civic Duty
articles.content:
Every tax return preparer probably has a few clients who complain about not being able to pay their tax bill. This usually is the case because of poor tax planning, forgetting to make quarterly tax payments, or because someone either partied too hard or had to get the roof fixed. But this year, I’ve heard of an increase of complaints from clients who cannot pay their taxes because of the effect of inflation.
Inflation rearranges household priorities. When the prices of groceries, rent or mortgage payments, utilities, gasoline, and insurance climb faster than income, eventually something must be cut. Because ordinary living expenses are in most cases not tax deductible, they reduce disposable cash without reducing taxable income. When the tax bill arrives, the taxpayer may not have the money to pay it.
This situation usually affects self-employed people, including those working contractor or gig jobs. Since they are paid in full, it is their responsibility to withhold taxes. But sometimes, W-2 employees can be in this situation as well. If they are used to getting tax refunds, they may adjust their withholdings to get a lower refund or pay taxes later.
The usual scenarios for not paying taxes mentioned above are usually temporary or a one-time mistake. They get back on track moving forward and pay the back taxes plus interest. If they can convince the tax collectors that they had reasonable cause for not paying the tax, then penalties can be waived.
Every tax professional or financial advisor will tell people facing this problem to pay their quarterly taxes or withhold more taxes, stop eating avocado toast, quit the vaping, and cancel their streaming subscriptions. Obviously that is easier said than done, and the last thing a person facing financial struggles needs is a lecture.
The problem with inflation is that it is not temporary. Someone can only hope that inflation stays at a manageable level and that their income will rise enough to cover it. Many people justify deferring taxes because other creditors can take more immediate action such as shutting down utilities, eviction, foreclosure, car repossessions, or lawsuits. Also, not eating really sucks.
So instead of a lecture on austerity, here is some practical advice coming from the perspective of someone who has dealt with tax collectors.
First, file your tax returns on time, even if you owe. If you do not file on time, you could pay a very large nonfiling penalty. Also, the IRS in recent years has been clamping down on nonfilers. Even if you miss one year, there is a good chance the IRS will send you a reminder letter. And if you want to set up a payment plan, you will be required to file all outstanding tax returns.
Second, if you owe, try to set up a payment plan as soon as possible. Even if you are not in a formal installment agreement, try to pay what you can every month. This can avoid further enforced tax collection action. However, make sure that your payment plans leaves you with enough money to pay future taxes and stop the bleeding.
Third, have a plan to get back into tax compliance while dealing with inflation. For self-employed people, you will need to find a way to increase revenue or decrease expenses. W-2 employees will need to adjust their W-4 withholdings. This may require people to make lifestyle changes, but you will have some time before the next tax return is due.
Lastly, while the IRS and most state tax agencies have an Offer in Compromise program where you can settle your back taxes for less than you owe, don’t be in a rush. You must first be able to pay taxes and file returns on time in the future. Otherwise, a settlement offer will not be considered. Second, consult with a tax professional as they know whether a settlement offer will be accepted in light of your financial situation both in the present and the future.
Over the past few years, inflation has hurt the purchasing power of the average American. It is tempting to put taxes on hold if you are facing eviction or starvation. But eventually the tax collectors will come get you, and they have formidable powers. So long as you file tax returns on time and try to pay down the tax debt, most tax agencies should give you some time to get your life back on track. Conversely, the federal and state governments should be willing to give struggling taxpayers some breathing room while they try to deal with inflation.
Steven Chung is a tax attorney in Los Angeles, California. He helps people with basic tax planning and resolve tax disputes. He is also sympathetic to people with large student loans. He can be reached via email at stevenchungatl@gmail.com. Or you can connect with him on Twitter (@stevenchung) and connect with him on LinkedIn.
The post Food, Shelter, Or Taxes: How Inflation Is Making Making Taxpayers Choose Between Survival And Their Civic Duty appeared first on Above the Law.

articles.title: DOJ Threatens ABA With Antitrust Probe Over… Adjunct Professors
articles.content:
The Trump administration’s long war on the American Bar Association has opened a new front, and it’s… adjunct professors. According to The Wall Street Journal, the Justice Department has warned the ABA that it could face an antitrust investigation unless it loosens the accreditation rules limiting how much part-time faculty can teach law students.
The warning came in an Oct. 7 letter from Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward, the DOJ’s No. 3 and before that Walt Nauta’s defense lawyer in Trump’s classified documents case, to the ABA’s Council of the Section of Legal Education and Admissions to the Bar, the arm of the organization that actually accredits law schools. Woodward’s argument is that adjuncts are cheaper, often bring more real-world experience, and that capping their teaching load hurts legal education and pushes tuition up. The DOJ’s theory of legal education, apparently, is that knowing how to teach is the one qualification a law professor doesn’t need, and that a career spent learning how 1Ls actually learn is just a cost to cut. He gave the council 15 days to change the standard or explain why it doesn’t violate federal antitrust law. If the answer is deemed “insufficient,” the department “may proceed with additional investigatory steps necessary to address the apparent violation of federal antitrust law.”
Woodward also wrote that the standard appears to restrict his own ability to teach first-year students. Woodward, per his DOJ biography, is an adjunct law professor at Catholic University.
So, is that the issue? One senior Justice Department official who’d like a crack at the 1Ls? Or is it just another way for MAGAland to take a swipe at the ABA for the unforgivable sin of suing the White House (over its campaign against Biglaw and then asking for the receipts).
Last month, the council proposed eliminating its requirement that full-time faculty teach the first third of the curriculum, while still requiring full-timers to cover more than half of a school’s credit hours or two-thirds of student contact hours. Woodward’s letter says that won’t fully resolve the department’s concerns, and a spokeswoman for the council says it plans to respond.
If the “comply, and then get told it isn’t enough” routine sounds familiar, that’s because the ABA has been living it since the start of Trump 2.0. Then-Attorney General Pam Bondi demanded the ABA scrap its diversity standard back in early 2025 or risk losing its accreditor status. The ABA suspended Standard 206, extended the suspension, moved to repeal it, and finally killed it outright. Its reward? The Education Department moved to yank the ABA’s accreditor role anyway on the same day the council was voting to surrender. Meanwhile, the FTC blamed high law school tuition on ABA accreditation and started leaning on state supreme courts to stop relying on it, and Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton launched his own investigation into the ABA’s accreditation practices earlier this month.
The ABA thought it could buy peace by dropping Standard 206, but this administration isn’t (just) trying to end diversity — it’s also punishing institutions that oppose them.

articles.title: AI Use In Law Firms: There’s Reality. And There’s What Management Wants It To Be.
articles.content:
Haven’t you heard? Everyone is using AI. All the time. Depending on which survey you read, somewhere between half and nearly 70% of lawyers and legal professionals are using AI.
But I sometimes wonder about those surveys. Many are commissioned by vendors selling Gen AI and AI products. So, it’s in their interest that the numbers appear high. That’s not to say that they are being purposely misleading, but we all know the way you ask the survey question can influence the answer. And it’s hard to know what is really going on in offices behind closed doors versus what people say is going on. So a little skepticism is in order.
And there’s another thing. When I go to speak at or attend conferences, I typically engage the room about AI use. And the number of hands raised by those admitting use always seems to be substantially less than what the surveys suggest. It’s anecdotal, but I attend enough conferences and speak at enough conferences that it’s noticeable.
Introducing Performative AI
Perhaps another factor is at play. It’s the notion of performative AI. The practice of exaggerating AI use and expertise to satisfy either employers or clients. Lawyers becoming experts at looking like AI experts. I hadn’t thought of this until a recent report from an outfit called Visier came out.
Visier is a Canadian company that specializes in people analytics, workforce intelligence, and AI-powered human resources management. It is also known for publishing research about workforce trends, employee behavior, including the gap between what employees say they are doing and what they actually are. So, if anyone has an idea of what’s really going on in the hallowed halls, it’s these guys.
The report and survey do not claim to have been directed at legal. But it’s an understatement to say that law firms could certainly use some help in areas which Visier covers. Most firms don’t even understand project management or workflows. Much less how their people are reacting to management-imposed changes.
The Report And Headline
Visier’s report of its survey was interesting. It surveyed some 1,000 full-time U.S. employees and asked them how they used AI in their day-to-day work. And what they thought about their organization’s AI strategy. It then interviewed a number of employees who work in various fields like healthcare, finance, HR, software, and others. The Visier summary of the research is entitled “AI in the Workplace: New Research on Performative AI.”
And here’s the key headline: 48% of employees say they have exaggerated AI usage or expertise to either colleagues or leadership. Forty-eight percent! That’s a lot. Visier puts it this way: “For these employees, performative AI feels safer than admitting they’re still learning.”
But Law Firms Are Special Snowflakes, Right?
I can just hear law firm management. We are different. We know what our people are up to. But Visier’s survey and interviews spanned enough industries that could each claim they, too, were different from one another. Indeed, the pressures Visier found weren’t confined to one industry. Visier does note that how AI plays out varies by role and function, but the core dynamic of the pressure to perform and leaders who don’t see it showed up across the board.
And as far as law firms being different, I don’t buy it. Lawyers have an innate independent streak. They find a way to do or not do something, and they adopt it. Damn the torpedoes. I’ve seen it over and over. And when a new piece of tech comes in and lawyers are supposed to use it, many just don’t. And management often doesn’t take the time to investigate. How long did it take most firms to get all the lawyers to migrate their files to the cloud as opposed to their individual on-prem folders? (I daresay some of them probably still have on-prem files at home.)
So when surveys are taken of law firm leaders about AI use of those in the firm, there’s every reason to think that a similar percentage are exaggerating use in their law firms as well. The same pressures apply.
The leaders answering the survey may simply not know it. They want to believe that their lawyers are using the newfangled AI toys management bought. Which means the survey statistics about lawyer and legal professional AI use that we are seeing may be inflated as well.
But There’s More. A Lot More
The report also reveals a whole lot more that could be informative to law firms. Visier puts it this way: “Performative AI has become a coping mechanism for a workforce that has been handed a mandate without a map.” Sounds like a lot of law firms.
And it’s supported by Visier’s statistics. 45% of employees feel pressure to use AI at work, even though they are not confident they know how to use it effectively. Also sounds familiar.
Visier sees a pattern of visible compliance over real AI adoption and integration. “Employees also rate leadership understanding of AI at work low across the board.” Only 33% believe leaders understand how much training and support are needed. Only 29% believe leaders recognize employee concerns about AI. A scant 28% believe that their leaders fully understand how employees use AI today.
It gets even more depressing. In previous research, Visier found that 56% called AI skill alignment critical, but just 15% said their workplace planning is keeping up. And in the current survey, employees said they want more AI training and upskilling, and more transparency from leadership. But they aren’t getting it.
That clearly reflects a mismatch between what employees are doing and what leadership thinks. Which no doubt contributes to the performative AI phenomenon.
Are we creating an environment where people can’t admit they don’t know how to use AI for fear that they’ll look incompetent?
Then There Is Law Firm Management
Lest we think that the situation is different for law firms, we only have to look at recent research from Harbor Global to see a similar scenario. Law firms investing in AI without coming up with ways to measure an impact. Which suggests a similar phenomenon to that found by Visier is in fact occurring in law firms.
The pressures are the same for law firm management as in other businesses. Law firms are notorious for buying software, announcing strategies, and congratulating themselves on their progress. Management so wants to believe (and have the rest of the partners believe) the AI investments are paying off. And let’s face it, transparency is not a strong suit of most law firms.
Given all this, law firm management would be wise to study the Visier findings. There could very well be the same performative AI going on in law firms, just as in most other businesses. Somewhere down the hall, there’s a lawyer (or two, or three) quietly doing things exactly the way they did them five years ago. Except now they tell management and maybe even their clients they’re using AI.
That does not lead to a happy ending. Sooner or later, clients are going to figure it out. Sooner or later, they will want more than a PowerPoint about their firm’s transition. They’re going to want results. Efficiencies.
There’s an internal cost too. The gap between what employees need and want and what leadership knows and plans for does not bode well for employee retention. Especially at a time when so many law firms are trying to attract and retain talent.
The Reality Gap
I can’t help but think there is a critical mismatch between what vendors want to believe is going on, what law firm leaders think is going on, and what is actually going on. This could explain many of the blank looks in the room when vendors or consultants talk about things like AI skills or agentic AI.
It’s always helpful when law firm leadership gets outside its own box. When it reviews information available from other domains and sources. Alas, that rarely happens.
So before firms go all in on AI, maybe they should pause and reflect on what the Visier report is saying about what is really going on. About reality, not what management thinks or wants it to be.
Otherwise, all those new AI toys will stay shiny. Because nobody has a clue how to use them. They just say they do.
Stephen Embry is a lawyer, speaker, blogger, and writer. He publishes TechLaw Crossroads, a blog devoted to the examination of the tension between technology, the law, and the practice of law.
The post AI Use In Law Firms: There’s Reality. And There’s What Management Wants It To Be. appeared first on Above the Law.

The report also reveals a whole lot more that could be informative to law firms. Visier puts it this way: “Performative AI has become a coping mechanism for a workforce that has been handed a mandate without a map.” Sounds like a lot of law firms. 

And it’s supported by Visier’s statistics. 45% of employees feel pressure to use AI at work, even though they are not confident they know how to use it effectively. Also sounds familiar.

Visier sees a pattern of visible compliance over real AI adoption and integration. “Employees also rate leadership understanding of AI at work low across the board.” Only 33% believe leaders understand how much training and support are needed. Only 29% believe leaders recognize employee concerns about AI. A scant 28% believe that their leaders fully understand how employees use AI today. 

It gets even more depressing. In previous research, Visier found that 56% called AI skill alignment critical, but just 15% said their workplace planning is keeping up. And in the current survey, employees said they want more AI training and upskilling, and more transparency from leadership. But they aren’t getting it.

That clearly reflects a mismatch between what employees are doing and what leadership thinks. Which no doubt contributes to the performative AI phenomenon. 

Are we creating an environment where people can’t admit they don’t know how to use AI for fear that they’ll look incompetent?

Then There Is Law Firm Management

Lest we think that the situation is different for law firms, we only have to look at recent research from Harbor Global to see a similar scenario. Law firms investing in AI without coming up with ways to measure an impact. Which suggests a similar phenomenon to that found by Visier is in fact occurring in law firms.

The pressures are the same for law firm management as in other businesses. Law firms are notorious for buying software, announcing strategies, and congratulating themselves on their progress. Management so wants to believe (and have the rest of the partners believe) the AI investments are paying off. And let’s face it, transparency is not a strong suit of most law firms. 

Given all this, law firm management would be wise to study the Visier findings. There could very well be the same performative AI going on in law firms, just as in most other businesses.  Somewhere down the hall, there’s a lawyer (or two, or three) quietly doing things exactly the way they did them five years ago. Except now they tell management and maybe even their clients they’re using AI.

That does not lead to a happy ending. Sooner or later, clients are going to figure it out. Sooner or later, they will want more than a PowerPoint about their firm’s transition. They’re going to want results. Efficiencies.

There’s an internal cost too. The gap between what employees need and want and what leadership knows and plans for does not bode well for employee retention. Especially at a time when so many law firms are trying to attract and retain talent.

The Reality Gap

I can’t help but think there is a critical mismatch between what vendors want to believe is going on, what law firm leaders think is going on, and what is actually going on. This could explain many of the blank looks in the room when vendors or consultants talk about things like AI skills or agentic AI. 

It’s always helpful when law firm leadership gets outside its own box. When it reviews information available from other domains and sources. Alas, that rarely happens. 

So before firms go all in on AI, maybe they should pause and reflect on what the Visier report is saying about what is really going on. About reality, not what management thinks or wants it to be.

Otherwise, all those new AI toys will stay shiny. Because nobody has a clue how to use them. They just say they do.
